findings.claim: The custom Merkle tree duplicates Git's native tree architecture, violating the `adopt before build` mandate while adding unnecessary risk.
evidence: Git inherently constructs a Merkle tree over the repository's files. A signed Git tag provides a cryptographically secure Merkle set-commitment over the store.

Adopting a signed Git tag alone eliminates 418 lines of custom cryptography. The only property lost is layout-independence, but the test suite ('packet moved to the store root -> VERIFIED') shows layout is not strictly enforced anyway.
findings.falsifier: Git's Merkle tree fails to satisfy a specific cryptographic constraint strictly required by the threat model that the custom tree successfully provides.

findings.claim: Dynamically sorting leaves by `(identity, int(sequence), said)` destroys the append-only nature of the tree, making efficient consistency proofs mathematically impossible.
evidence: Sorting leaves dynamically rather than appending chronologically means adding a new identity inserts a leaf into the middle of the Merkle tree.
This completely alters all internal nodes above it, breaking the structural requirements for log consistency proofs (RFC 6962).
Consequently, verifying `ANCHOR_STALE` requires downloading the entire store to rebuild the tree from scratch, rendering the Merkle architecture no better than a flat signed hash of the sorted store.
findings.falsifier: The implementation includes a novel zero-knowledge or structural proof that can efficiently demonstrate one dynamically sorted Merkle tree is a strict superset of another without transmitting the full leaf set.

findings.claim: If the BLAKE3-256 root is used exactly as the Git tag name, major Git platforms will reject the push due to commit hash ambiguity rules.
findings.location: scripts/provenance_anchor.py (Publication argument: 'root is placed in the git tag name')
evidence: GitLab documentation explicitly states: 'Tag names starting with 40 or 64 hexadecimal characters are prohibited, because they are similar to Git commit hashes' [5.2.1].
GitHub similarly prohibits pushes of tags that are exactly 40 hex characters long.
A bare BLAKE3-256 root (64 hex characters) pushed without a prefix will fail on these hosts.
findings.falsifier: The `provenance_anchor.py` script automatically prefixes the tag name (e.g., `anchor-<root>`) to avoid git ref format collisions.

findings.claim: The fallback mechanism that records locked files as `unreadable[]` allows an attacker to mask head truncation by locking files instead of deleting them.
evidence: On Windows, concurrent processes can place exclusive locks on files, raising `PermissionError` on read.
If the anchor script handles this by appending the file to `unreadable[]` and excluding it from the Merkle tree, an attacker can hold a lock on truncated packets during the anchor run.
The Merkle root will silently omit those packets, bypassing truncation detection without explicitly altering the store.
findings.falsifier: The verification logic treats the presence of any entry in `unreadable[]` as an immediate fatal error rather than a logged warning when evaluating `ANCHOR_STALE` or `VERIFIED`.

findings.claim: The assumption that pushing a git tag creates an immutable fact on third-party mirrors ignores the race condition of immediate deletion.
evidence: An operator acting maliciously can execute `git push origin tagname && git push --delete origin tagname`.
Since third-party mirrors (like GHArchive) operate on a polling interval or queue, the tag can be destroyed before it is ingested, leaving no external fact.
A transparency log (e.g., Sigstore Rekor) is strictly required to synchronously witness the event.
findings.falsifier: The project relies on a verified webhook integration that synchronously commits pushed tags to an immutable ledger before returning HTTP 200 to the git client.

findings.claim: The tree construction strictly violates RFC 6962 by promoting odd nodes layer-by-layer instead of using power-of-2 balancing.
findings.location: docs/specs/provenance-anchor.spec.md ('RFC 6962-shaped binary Merkle... odd node promoted')
evidence: RFC 6962 Section 2.1 dictates partitioning leaves at the largest power of 2 (k < n) and recursively hashing. It does not promote odd nodes layer-by-layer.
Layer-by-layer odd node promotion fundamentally modifies the tree shape, guaranteeing that standard RFC 6962 verifiers and proof libraries will compute a mismatched root.
findings.falsifier: The specification intends to refer only to the domain separators (0x00, 0x01) of RFC 6962, not the structural shape, and expects clients to use the custom verifier logic exclusively.

predicted_majority: Other reviewers will likely focus on the operational weaknesses of the Python script (e.g., Windows filesystem locks, clock skew) and the lack of true non-repudiation in Git tag publication.
where_you_expect_to_be_alone: Identifying that dynamically sorting the leaves by identity and sequence completely destroys the ability to generate Merkle consistency proofs, making the custom Merkle tree architecture functionally identical to a flat hash.
